title: Signaling Dynamics
terms: How a cell gets the right amount of signal: amplify it, measure it, and modify it with agonists or antagonists.
★ Dr. Schultz's classic pathways (steroid, Gs/Gi/Gq, tyrosine kinase, guanylyl cyclase): "really good if you ... could walk through those pathways." Pharmacology expects it.
Pathways are GRADIENTS, not on/off: more or less signal gives more or less effect.
Adrenal tumor secreting catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, some dopamine) → extreme sympathetic signal everywhere; poking it in surgery releases more.
Epinephrine, norepinephrine, and (to some degree) dopamine.
Blood pressure swinging wildly ("sometimes 800/600, sometimes 0/0") from catecholamine surges; both extremes inconsistent with life.
Going from a very low signal concentration to a relatively large cell effect, via second messenger steps.
★ Intracellular signal after the primary signal; allows AMPLIFICATION, MODULATION, and INTEGRATION. Gs → cAMP; Gi → ↓ cAMP; Gq → IP3 and/or DAG.
Gs → cAMP; Gi → ↓ cAMP; Gq → IP3/DAG
★ "Memorize in your sleep": Gs second messenger = cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP); Gi = NOT cAMP (↓); Gq = inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and/or diacylglycerol (DAG).
Steroid hormone receptor itself goes to the nucleus as a transcription factor; example of signaling without second messengers.
Second-messenger steps (G proteins, kinases, phosphatases) let the cell turn the signal up or down.
Primary signal acts directly: 1:1 signal-to-effect, limited by receptor number and signal concentration, cannot integrate; "literally an on-off system."
With second messengers, one primary signal produces far more than one unit of effect.
Other signals merge into the same second-messenger pathway: two Gs signals synergize, a Gi signal counteracts; one decision point.
Glucagon + epinephrine together both raise cAMP → liver breaks down glycogen "really, really fast."
A Gi signal on the same cell counteracts Gs → less effect than Gs alone.
Glucagon, epinephrine, insulin, glucocorticoids, growth hormone, AMP:ATP status, citrate — integrated into one glycogen phosphorylase decision.
Liver glucagon and epinephrine receptors are both Gs-coupled. Receptor acts as guanine nucleotide exchange factor: GDP out, GTP in; αs leaves βγ → adenylyl cyclase.
Enzyme activated by Gs; converts adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
Second messenger made by adenylyl cyclase; activates protein kinase A.
cAMP-activated kinase; phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase in the liver cell cascade.
Kinase phosphorylated by PKA; phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase.
Enzyme activated by phosphorylase kinase; breaks glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate.
End product of the liver Gs cascade; released from glycogen by glycogen phosphorylase.
Each activated molecule keeps acting while active: receptor (while agonist bound), Gαs (while GTP bound), PKA (while cAMP bound), each kinase (while phosphorylated).
Total amplification from very-low-concentration epinephrine/glucagon to glucose-1-phosphate in a liver cell.
★ Receptors respond to CHANGES in signal concentration, not absolute concentration; sustained signal → less and less effect.
Chronic opioid users (medical or recreational) need more and more for the same effect → can lead to overdose as other pathways overactivate.
Airway smooth muscle relaxant (e.g. albuterol); daily use desensitizes, so daily asthma maintenance uses a glucocorticoid instead.
Short-term loss of response (slide: milliseconds–minutes). Basel: some systems desensitize within milliseconds–seconds.
Long-term loss of response (slide: days–years; Basel: hours to days and longer).
Fast desensitization: a kinase PHOSPHORYLATES the receptor (seconds–minutes) and arrestin binds, blocking signaling.
Protein that binds phosphorylated receptors and blocks signaling (seconds–minutes); accompanies receptor internalization.
Receptors pulled off the membrane (internalized) into vesicles → degraded or recycled. Basel groups it with hours–days changes.
Cell makes fewer receptors (hours–days) so it stays sensitive to changes, not absolute signal.
Long-term deactivation of insulin receptors can lead toward type 2 diabetes. Basel unsure of exact kinetics (see flag).
S9 figure: G-protein signal (<~1 s) → phosphorylation → arrestin binding → endocytosis (~10 min–1 hr); resensitization or recycling afterward.
Kinase on the S9 timeline that phosphorylates the agonist-bound receptor within seconds (expansion of GRK is OUTSIDE — confirm).
Arrestin shown on S9 binding the phosphorylated receptor (~seconds to minutes) before endocytosis.
S9 recovery routes: phosphorylated surface receptor resensitizes quickly; endocytosed receptor returns by recycling.
Effect = Emax × [ligand] / (EC50 + [ligand]). Applies to receptor AND enzyme pathways. ★ "I don't need you to do math."
Little agonist + many free receptors → sharp rise in effect; as receptors fill, less effect per added agonist; saturated → no further change.
On/off binding rates (Dr. Schultz). Many free receptors → high Kon; as receptors fill, Kon falls until Koff balances it.
Ligand = anything that binds a receptor (agnostic to effect). Agonist = ligand that ACTIVATES it.
Maximal possible effect (all receptors maximally active); only at infinite concentration, so never actually reached. Measure of efficacy.
★ Concentration giving ½ Emax; tells how sensitive the pathway is to the signal. ALWAYS has concentration units.
★ = Emax: how much effect you could get at very high signal. Higher Emax = more efficacious; curve shifts UP.
★ = EC50: how much signal is needed for the effect. LOWER EC50 = MORE potent; curve shifts LEFT.
★ Linear effect vs log [ligand] (each unit = ×10). Sigmoid curve; easy to read Emax and EC50. "Make sure you can read a semi-log plot."
Hyperbola with EC50s clustered in the corner; used only for thought experiments ("last time you'll see this").
A ligand that ACTIVATES the receptor (a type of ligand); has measurable potency and efficacy.
Activates maximal response equal to the endogenous ligand.

traps: Efficacy = Emax (how big the maximum is); potency = EC50 (how much drug is needed). Do not swap them.
More potent = LOWER EC50; less potent = HIGHER EC50. Lower number wins.
Competitive antagonist raises EC50 (curve shifts right, Emax kept); non-competitive antagonist lowers Emax.
Competitive antagonism is overcome by more agonist because agonist competes for binding sites; it does not kick the antagonist out.
Partial agonist = less than maximal response (can antagonize stronger agonists); super agonist = greater than endogenous full agonist; inverse agonist = opposite effect, needs basal activity.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: an antagonist blocks an agonist; an inverse agonist produces the opposite effect on its own (needs basal signaling).
Reversible = measurable koff; irreversible = no measurable koff. An irreversible antagonist looks non-competitive regardless of where it binds.
Naloxone (competitive, opioid receptor) vs ketamine (non-competitive, NMDA receptor). Buprenorphine = partial agonist, not antagonist.
Adenylyl cyclase (enzyme, -ase) makes cAMP from ATP; phosphorylase kinase activates glycogen phosphorylase (kinase comes first).
★ Second messengers: Gs → cAMP ↑; Gi → NOT cAMP (↓); Gq → IP3 and/or DAG. Steroid receptors have NO second messenger (receptor = transcription factor) (transcript).
★ Shift directions: more efficacious = curve shifts UP (higher Emax); more potent = shifts LEFT (lower EC50). Less potent = right; less efficacious = down (transcript, S12–S14).
★ EC50 units = CONCENTRATION (not % effect, not time). Read it by tracing from ½ Emax down to the x-axis (transcript, S14).
Ligand ≠ agonist: ligand just binds (agnostic); agonist ACTIVATES. Every agonist is a ligand, not vice versa (transcript).
Desensitization mechanisms by speed: receptor phosphorylation and arrestin = seconds–minutes; internalization / reduced expression = hours–days (transcript).
Emax is never actually reached (requires infinite agonist). Receptors respond to changes, not absolute concentration (transcript, S7, S11).

quiz.stem: In a liver cell, very-low-concentration epinephrine signals through the stimulatory G protein (Gs) cascade to release glucose-1-phosphate. Per the slide, the total amplification is about:
quiz.why: S6 labels the whole cascade ~100,000,000-fold; Basel: 100 × 100 × 10 × 10 × 100 (transcript).

quiz.stem: Compared with a direct-effect signal (1:1 ratio), second messengers allow which three things?
quiz.ok: Amplification, integration, and modulation
bad: Amplification, desensitization, and tolerance
Integration, internalization, and inhibition
Modulation, phosphorylation, and degradation
quiz.why: S4–S5 + transcript: second messengers allow amplification, modulation, and integration.

quiz.stem: In the liver stimulatory G protein (Gs) cascade, which enzyme directly activates glycogen phosphorylase?
quiz.ok: Phosphorylase kinase
bad: Protein kinase A (PKA)
Adenylyl cyclase
Stimulatory G protein (Gs)
quiz.why: S6: protein kinase A (PKA) → phosphorylase kinase → glycogen phosphorylase → glucose-1-phosphate.

quiz.stem: A receptor stays on the cell surface but is phosphorylated by a kinase and bound by arrestin, giving much less effect for the same signal. Which desensitization method is this?
quiz.ok: Disabled signaling
bad: Membrane cycling
Reduced expression
Competitive antagonism
quiz.why: S8: disabled signaling = kinase phosphorylation + arrestin binding at the surface; membrane cycling internalizes the receptor.

quiz.stem: An asthmatic cat on a long-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist shows a falling bronchodilator response over several months. Per the slide's terms, this long-term loss is called:
quiz.ok: Tolerance
bad: Desensitization
Partial agonism
Inverse agonism
quiz.why: S7: short term (milliseconds–minutes) = desensitization; long term (days–years) = tolerance.

quiz.stem: On a Michaelis-Menten dose-response curve, efficacy and potency are described by which parameters?
quiz.ok: Efficacy by Emax; potency by EC50
bad: Efficacy by EC50; potency by Emax
Efficacy by koff; potency by Emax
Efficacy by Emax; potency by koff
quiz.why: S10, S12–S13: efficacy = maximal effect (Emax); potency = EC50.

quiz.stem: Drug A has Emax 100 and EC50 100. Drug B has Emax 100 and EC50 25. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Drug B is more potent and equally efficacious
bad: Drug B is more efficacious and equally potent
Drug B is less potent and equally efficacious
Drug B is less efficacious and more potent
quiz.why: S13: same Emax, lower EC50 = more potent.

quiz.stem: Drug A has Emax 100 and EC50 100. Drug C has Emax 150 and EC50 100. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Drug C is more efficacious and equally potent
bad: Drug C is more potent and equally efficacious
Drug C is less efficacious and equally potent
Drug C is more potent and less efficacious
quiz.why: S12: same EC50, higher Emax = more efficacious.

quiz.stem: A dog receiving high-dose morphine is given buprenorphine. Based on the slide, what happens to the mu-opioid receptor response?
quiz.ok: It falls; buprenorphine acts as an antagonist
bad: It rises; buprenorphine acts as a super agonist
It reverses; buprenorphine acts as an inverse agonist
It is unchanged; they bind different sites
quiz.why: S19: buprenorphine is a partial agonist; partial agonists can act as antagonists against more efficacious agonists.

quiz.stem: Goserelin is used in prostate and breast cancer. At the luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone receptor (LHRHR) it acts as a:
quiz.ok: Super agonist that downregulates the receptor
bad: Partial agonist that blocks the receptor
Competitive antagonist that blocks the receptor
Inverse agonist that silences basal activity
quiz.why: S19: goserelin is an LHRHR super agonist used to downregulate LHRHR and sex hormone production.

quiz.stem: For an inverse agonist to produce a measurable effect, the receptor must have:
quiz.ok: Basal signaling activity with no agonist bound
bad: An allosteric site occupied by an antagonist
Phosphorylation by a kinase and arrestin bound
A covalent bond to an irreversible ligand
quiz.why: S18: inverse agonism is often caused by receptors that have basal signaling activity with no agonist.

quiz.stem: With an antagonist present, the agonist curve shifts right, but enough agonist still reaches the full Emax. Which drug best fits this pattern?
quiz.ok: Naloxone at the opioid receptor
bad: Ketamine at the NMDA receptor
Buprenorphine at the opioid receptor
Ro15-4513 at the GABA receptor
quiz.why: S21: competitive antagonist (naloxone) raises EC50 and is overcome by more agonist. Ketamine lowers Emax; buprenorphine (partial agonist) caps the max; Ro15-4513 is an inverse agonist. NMDA = N-methyl-D-aspartate; GABA = gamma-aminobutyric acid.

quiz.stem: In the slide's lock-and-key model, a car boot that stops the car whether or not a key is in the ignition represents a:
quiz.ok: Non-competitive antagonist
bad: Competitive antagonist
Partial agonist
Inverse agonist
quiz.why: S17: car boot = non-competitive antagonist binding an allosteric site; key blank = competitive antagonist.

quiz.stem: Per the slide, raising agonist concentration overcomes a competitive antagonist by:
quiz.ok: Competing with it for binding sites
bad: Kicking it off its binding site
Binding the allosteric site instead
Lowering the antagonist's off rate
quiz.why: S21: more agonist does not kick out the antagonist but competes for binding sites; ability depends partly on antagonist k-1.

quiz.stem: An antagonist binds the agonist binding site but has essentially no measurable off rate (koff). Its dose-response effect will look like:
quiz.ok: A non-competitive antagonist, lowering Emax
bad: A competitive antagonist, raising EC50
A partial agonist, lowering EC50
An inverse agonist, reversing the effect
quiz.why: S22: an irreversible antagonist (actual or practical) looks non-competitive regardless of where it binds.

quiz.stem: Using the slide's off rates (koff), which ligand has the shortest receptor residence time?
quiz.ok: Acetylcholine, koff ~1000/s
bad: Morphine, koff ~0.01/s
Antibodies, koff ~0.001/s
Irreversible inhibitor, koff ~1/s
quiz.why: S22: acetylcholine has low/sub-millisecond residence times (koff ~1000/s), the fastest off rate listed.

quiz.stem: A dog with a pheochromocytoma is prepped for surgery. Why is phenoxybenzamine chosen to prevent norepinephrine-driven hemodynamic instability?
quiz.ok: Irreversible non-competitive alpha blockade lowers Emax
bad: Competitive alpha blockade raises the EC50
Partial alpha agonism lowers the EC50
Inverse alpha agonism silences basal activity
quiz.why: S24: a non-competitive inhibitor should reduce maximum epinephrine response no matter the dose; phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible, non-competitive alpha-adrenergic inhibitor.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT a method of receptor desensitization shown on the slide?
quiz.ok: Inverse agonism
bad: Disabled signaling
Membrane cycling
Reduced expression
quiz.why: S8 lists three methods: disabled signaling (kinase + arrestin), membrane cycling, reduced expression. Inverse agonism is a ligand type (S18).

quiz.stem: Per lecture, why do Gs-coupled pathways use second messengers instead of a direct receptor effect?
quiz.ok: To amplify, modulate, and integrate the incoming signal
bad: To keep a strict one-to-one signal-to-effect ratio
To limit the effect to the receptor number present
To let the receptor itself act as a transcription factor
quiz.why: Second messengers expand a small signal (amplification), allow regulation (modulation), and let other signals merge (integration). Direct effect = 1:1, receptor-limited; steroid receptors act as transcription factors.

quiz.stem: A receptor is exposed to a sustained agonist. Which pairing of desensitization mechanism and time scale matches the lecture?
quiz.ok: Arrestin binding blocks the receptor within seconds to minutes
bad: Receptor internalization removes surface receptors within a few milliseconds
Reduced receptor expression lowers signaling within seconds to minutes
Receptor phosphorylation lowers signaling only over days to years
quiz.why: Phosphorylation and arrestin act within seconds–minutes; internalization and reduced expression take hours–days.

quiz.stem: On a semi-log dose-response plot, Drug B's curve sits to the LEFT of Drug A's with the same plateau. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Drug B is more potent, with a lower EC50
bad: Drug B is more efficacious, with a higher Emax
Drug B is less potent, with a higher EC50
Drug B is more potent, with a higher EC50
quiz.why: Left shift = lower EC50 = more potent; same plateau = same Emax (efficacy). Up shift would mean more efficacious.

quiz.stem: A student reads an EC50 off a semi-log plot by tracing from half of Emax down to the x-axis. In what units should the answer be reported?
quiz.ok: Concentration units, such as micromolar
bad: Effect units, such as percent response
Rate units, such as per second
Time units, such as minutes
quiz.why: EC50 is the concentration giving half-maximal effect, so it always has concentration units.

flags: "Michaelis-Menton" spelling
S10 says Michaelis-Menten; S11–S14 equation boxes say "Michaelis-Menton" · Use the correct spelling Michaelis-Menten.
CLOSED by transcript: Michaelis-Menten for receptors

Basel: Michaelis-Menten dynamics "happen in receptor signaling pathways. They happen in enzyme pathways." Use the slide's Emax/EC50 version; "I don't need you to do math" (equation won't be repeated).
Checked against slide image + transcript: S6 step multipliers

Image confirms: activated receptor → Gs ×100; adenylyl cyclase ATP → cAMP ×100; PKA → phosphorylase kinase ×10; phosphorylase kinase → glycogen phosphorylase ×10; glycogen → glucose-1-phosphate ×100 (no multiplier on cAMP → PKA); total ~100,000,000-fold. Transcript matches (groups cAMP → PKA without a multiplier; says "glucose residues" = glucose-1-phosphate). "Other signals" enter at PKA, phosphorylase kinase, glycogen phosphorylase.
CLOSED by transcript: S13 EC50 wording
S13 asks "How much drug is needed to get to maximal effect?"; Basel defines EC50 as "the effective concentration to get 50% of the maximal effect" (S11) · use half-maximal.
S19 heading vs drug list
S19 heading says "μ-opiod receptor acting drugs" (typo: opioid) but goserelin acts at the LHRH receptor and Ro15-4513 at the GABA receptor · Only morphine and buprenorphine are mu-opioid drugs.
Ro15-4513: inverse agonist vs "GABA antagonist"

S19 lists Ro15-4513 under Inverse Agonist; its parenthetical calls it a "GABA antagonist" ("antagonist" in red on the image) · Use inverse agonist (the slide's category). OUTSIDE — confirm: it acts at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor.
k-1 vs koff notation
S21 says "k-1 of antagonist"; S22 uses koff · Same quantity (dissociation/off rate). Treat as identical.
S22 practically irreversible koff overlaps morphine

Practically irreversible acetylcholine receptor inhibitor koff ~1/s–0.01/s overlaps morphine's ~0.01/s, which is reversible · "Practically irreversible" is relative to the endogenous ligand's speed (acetylcholine ~1000/s). Not yet lectured — confirm when covered.
Phenoxybenzamine binding site (OUTSIDE — confirm)

S24 calls it irreversible, non-competitive · Standard pharmacology: it alkylates (covalently binds) the alpha receptor; per S22 any irreversible antagonist behaves non-competitively regardless of site. Use slide wording.
Answered in LC30 (Wed 11/4): spare receptors

S24 asks why low-dose phenoxybenzamine shifts the curve right instead of depressing max · LC30 S26: there are spare alpha-adrenoceptors in many smooth muscles; low (tolerated) doses of the irreversible antagonist do not completely deplete the receptor reserve, so massive epinephrine can still cause hypertensive crisis. LC30 S27: the dose cannot just be raised because the therapeutic index is too small (full blockade is itself toxic).
S9 timeline vs transcript time scales

S9 figure: G-protein signal (<~1 s) → GRK phosphorylation → beta-arrestin-2 → endocytosis (~10 min–1 hr). S7: desensitization (ms–min) vs tolerance (days–years). Transcript: phosphorylation + arrestin seconds–minutes; internalization/reduced expression hours–days; "short term we call desensitization, long term we call tolerance" · use S7 two-term framing; for endocytosis timing, S9 (slides win), but know Basel grouped it with hours–days.
S24 citation typo
"Goodman & Gliman's" should be Goodman & Gilman's · Cosmetic only.

Student question: Basel said he would have to look up insulin specifically; long-term receptor deactivation can lead toward type 2 diabetes · do not rely on specific insulin kinetics.

Student answered "antagonist"; Basel then says "maybe we could give an agonist of some sort" right after saying we want to BLOCK adrenoreceptors · use antagonist (block adrenoreceptors); resolution not yet lectured.

Transcript lists "alpha 1s, alpha 2s, alpha 3s, beta 3s" · standard pharmacology has α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 — no α3; likely a slip. Not on slides.
Transcript slip: adenylyl cyclase "increase ATP"
Basel says αs increases adenylyl cyclase rate "and increase ATP" · S6: adenylyl cyclase converts ATP → cAMP (↑ cAMP). Use S6.
